description: Evaluates whether the skill correctly answers WCAG/a11y questions, generates proper ARIA code, explains standards accurately and gives actionable guidance. Responses are judged by meaning against each eval's `expectations`, not by keyword matching: an expectation can be met with different wording, and a keyword appearing in the response does not meet it (for example a date quoted as a future deadline does not meet an expectation that says the law already applies). Negative expectations ("Does not present X as...") fail if the response states X, even in passing.

evals.prompt:
My modal dialog closes when I press Escape but screen readers don't announce it as a dialog. What's wrong? Here's the code: ```html

Confirm Delete

Are you sure you want to delete this item?

```
evals.expected_output: Should identify that the container has no dialog semantics: add role="dialog" (or use a native <dialog> opened with showModal()), aria-modal="true" and a name through aria-labelledby pointing to the h2. Should say focus has to be managed: move focus into the dialog on open, keep Tab inside while it is modal, and return focus to the element that opened it on close. Should provide corrected code. May note that aria-modal alone does not trap focus or make the rest of the page inert (that is done with script, inert or showModal()).
expectations: Identifies that the container is missing dialog semantics and adds role="dialog" (or recommends the native <dialog> element with showModal()) in the corrected code.
Names the dialog by linking aria-labelledby to the h2 (or gives an equivalent accessible name), rather than leaving it unnamed.
Includes aria-modal="true" (or the native modal <dialog>) for a modal dialog.
Explains that focus must move into the dialog when it opens and return to the triggering element when it closes.
Provides corrected HTML that contains the dialog role and its name.
Does not claim that aria-modal="true" by itself keeps keyboard focus inside the dialog or disables the page behind it.

evals.prompt: What's the minimum color contrast ratio required for normal body text under WCAG 2.1 AA? My text is #6b7280 on #ffffff background. Does it pass?
evals.expected_output: Should state 4.5:1 as the AA minimum for normal text (SC 1.4.3). Should calculate the contrast of #6b7280 on #ffffff with the WCAG 2.x relative luminance formula: approximately 4.83:1 (4.8345 unrounded; rounding to 4.8 or 4.83 is fine). Should conclude that it passes AA for normal text, with a margin of about 0.33 above the threshold, and may note that it is close to the boundary and would not meet AAA (7:1). Must not report the 4.61:1 figure.
expectations: States that the minimum contrast ratio for normal-size text at Level AA is 4.5:1 and cites Success Criterion 1.4.3 or names it (Contrast (Minimum)).
Gives a computed contrast ratio for #6b7280 on #ffffff of about 4.83:1 (4.8 or 4.83 is fine).
Concludes that the pair passes AA for normal text.
If it mentions AAA, says the pair does not reach the 7:1 AAA ratio for normal text.
Does not report a ratio that is clearly different from about 4.83:1 (for example 4.61:1) and does not conclude that the pair fails AA.
sources: Computed with the WCAG relative luminance formula: (1.0 + 0.05) / (L(#6b7280) + 0.05) = 4.8345

evals.prompt: I'm building a custom dropdown menu in React. Users should be able to open it with Enter or Space, navigate options with arrow keys, and close with Escape. What ARIA attributes and keyboard behavior do I need?
evals.expected_output: The prompt is ambiguous: a control from which the user picks an option is a select-only combobox with a listbox popup (APG), while a button that opens a list of actions is a menu button with role="menu" (APG). A good answer says which pattern fits (choose a value: combobox + listbox; trigger actions: menu button), may suggest a native <select> when it is enough, and describes the matching attributes and keys. Combobox pattern: role="combobox" on the trigger, aria-expanded, aria-controls pointing to the role="listbox" popup, role="option" items, aria-activedescendant for the active option while focus stays on the combobox, accessible name. Keys per the APG select-only combobox: Down Arrow, Enter or Space open it; arrows move through the options; Enter or Space select; Escape closes; Home/End first/last; type-ahead. Menu button pattern: button with aria-haspopup="menu" (or true) and aria-expanded (aria-controls optional); Enter or Space opens and focuses the first item; roles menu/menuitem; Escape closes and returns focus to the button. role="menu" is for application actions, not for choosing a value or for site navigation. aria-haspopup is required on the menu button; the APG select-only combobox example does not use it.
expectations: Distinguishes the two patterns or states which one it assumes: choosing a value from options (combobox with a listbox popup, or a native <select>) versus opening a list of actions (menu button with role="menu"). It does not blend them into a single role set.

Gives the matching ARIA for the chosen pattern: for a combobox, role="combobox" with aria-expanded, aria-controls to a role="listbox" popup with role="option" items and aria-activedescendant (or roving focus) for the active option; for a menu button, aria-haspopup (menu or true) and aria-expanded on the button and menu/menuitem roles.
Describes the keyboard behavior asked for: Enter or Space opens it, arrow keys move between options, Escape closes it and focus ends on the trigger.
Mentions Home/End and/or type-ahead only as optional or additional keys, not as the core of the answer.
Does not recommend role="menu" for a control whose job is to select a value or for site navigation.
Does not say aria-haspopup is required on an APG select-only combobox.
sources: references/semantic-html-and-aria.md (role="menu" is for application menus, not site navigation)

evals.prompt: My company runs an online shop that sells to consumers in the EU. Do we need to be WCAG compliant? What standard applies and since when?
evals.expected_output: Should mention: European Accessibility Act (EAA, Directive (EU) 2019/882) and EN 301 549; that the EAA already applies since 28 June 2025 (present or past tense, not a future deadline); that it covers B2C digital products and services such as e-commerce; that EN 301 549 is the intended harmonised standard under the EAA, that v3.2.1 refers to WCAG 2.1 AA and is the version cited under the Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102, Decision (EU) 2021/1339), and that no version of EN 301 549 (neither v3.2.1 nor v4.1.1, which refers to WCAG 2.2) is confirmed as cited in the Official Journal of the EU under the EAA, so none should be presented as giving a presumption of conformity under it. Should recommend building to WCAG 2.2 AA (which also meets 2.1 AA, except that 4.1.1 Parsing is no longer in 2.2) and say this is general information, not legal advice. May mention the microenterprise exemption for services and the Art. 32 transitional measures.
expectations: States that the European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) already applies, since 28 June 2025, in the present or past tense. It does not present 28 June 2025 as an upcoming deadline or say the shop "will need" to comply by then.

Says the EAA covers consumer-facing (B2C) digital products and services such as e-commerce, so an online shop selling to EU consumers is in scope (it may add that micro-enterprises have an exemption for services).

Says EN 301 549 is the harmonised standard intended for the EAA, that version 3.2.1 refers to WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA for web content, and that v3.2.1 is the version cited under the Web Accessibility Directive.
Does not state that EN 301 549 v4.1.1 is already cited in the Official Journal of the EU or already gives a presumption of conformity; if it mentions v4.1.1, it says that citation is not confirmed.
Does not state that any version of EN 301 549 (neither v3.2.1 nor v4.1.1) is confirmed as cited in the Official Journal under the EAA or gives a presumption of conformity under it.
Recommends building to WCAG 2.2 AA (not only 2.1 AA), explaining that meeting 2.2 AA also covers 2.1 AA requirements.
States that this is general information and not legal advice, or tells the user to confirm with a lawyer or the official text.
Does not present the EAA as applying only to public-sector bodies, and does not present WCAG 2.2 AA as the legally mandated version in the EU today.
sources: data/legal-framework.csv (EAA row, EN 301 549 v3.2.1 and v4.1.1 rows, verified_on 2026-11-15)
DECISIONS.md (2026-11-14: WCAG 2.2 AA by default; 2.1 AA only if a law or contract names it)

evals.prompt: I want to add axe-core to my Playwright tests in a Next.js project. Can you give me a working setup with example test code?
evals.expected_output: Should provide: npm install of @axe-core/playwright, a test that imports AxeBuilder, navigates to a URL and runs analyze(), asserts that results.violations is empty (or reports them), uses withTags for the target level (for WCAG 2.2 AA: wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa, wcag22aa), and ideally integrates it into a CI check. Should say that automated tools find only part of the issues and manual checks are still needed. checkA11y belongs to other packages (cypress-axe, axe-playwright), not to @axe-core/playwright.
expectations: Installs and imports the official @axe-core/playwright package and uses AxeBuilder with a Playwright page.
Shows a test that navigates to a page, runs analyze() and asserts on or reports results.violations.
Restricts the rules to the target standard with withTags (including the WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 AA tags when targeting WCAG 2.2 AA), or explains why it does not.
Does not present the automated scan as proof of WCAG conformance; it says manual and assistive-technology testing is still needed.
Does not attribute a checkA11y function to @axe-core/playwright.

evals.prompt: How do I make my React Native app work with TalkBack on Android? I have a card component that shows an image, title, and price.
evals.expected_output: Should explain: make the card one accessible element (accessible={true} on the container, or use a Touchable, which is accessible by default) so TalkBack does not stop on each child; give it an accessibilityLabel that combines title and price (or let it derive from the children), accessibilityRole="button" (or "link") if tappable, accessibilityHint only for non-obvious results, a decorative image hidden from TalkBack, and a touch target of at least 48x48 dp (Android guidance; WCAG 2.5.8 AA is 24x24 CSS px, the 44x44 of 2.5.5 is AAA). Should provide a code example and say to test with TalkBack.
expectations: Groups the image, title and price into one focusable element for TalkBack (accessible on the container or a touchable component) instead of leaving three separate stops.
Gives the grouped element a combined accessibilityLabel (title and price) or explains how the label is derived from the children.
Sets the role to match the behavior (accessibilityRole or the equivalent role prop, for example button or link if the card is tappable).
Treats accessibilityHint as optional and for non-obvious results, not as a replacement for the label.
If it mentions touch target size, gives 48x48 dp as Android guidance and, if it cites WCAG, uses 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum, AA, 24x24 CSS px); it does not present 48 dp as a WCAG requirement.
Provides a React Native code example and recommends testing with TalkBack.

evals.prompt: What does WCAG 2.4.11 require? We just updated to WCAG 2.2 and I'm not sure what new criteria to check.
evals.expected_output: Should explain SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA: when a component receives keyboard focus it is not entirely hidden by author-created content such as sticky headers, footers or cookie banners. Should list the nine new WCAG 2.2 criteria with their levels: 2.4.11 AA, 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) AAA, 2.4.13 Focus Appearance AAA, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements AA, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA, 3.2.6 Consistent Help A, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry A, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) AA, 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) AAA. Should note that 4.1.1 Parsing is removed in WCAG 2.2.
expectations: Explains that 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) is Level AA and that the focused component must not be entirely hidden by author-created content such as a sticky header, footer or banner (partially hidden is allowed at AA).
Lists the other new WCAG 2.2 criteria (2.4.12, 2.4.13, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8, 3.3.9) or clearly says it is giving a partial list.
Gives levels that match the standard where it states them: 2.4.12, 2.4.13 and 3.3.9 are AAA; 2.5.7, 2.5.8 and 3.3.8 are AA; 3.2.6 and 3.3.7 are A.
Says 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in WCAG 2.2.
Does not describe 2.4.12 (Enhanced) as an AA requirement or say that 2.4.11 requires the focus indicator to have a minimum contrast ratio (that is 2.4.13, AAA).
sources: data/wcag-criteria.csv (ids and levels checked with scripts/search.py)

evals.prompt: My form validation shows errors in red text below each field, but a JAWS user told me they don't know the field has an error. How do I fix this?
evals.expected_output: Should recommend: put the error as text (3.3.1 Error Identification, A) and associate it with the field using aria-describedby; set aria-invalid="true" on the invalid input; make sure the error is conveyed without relying on color alone (1.4.1 Use of Color, A), for example with text or an icon with a text alternative; for errors that appear without a focus change (added after the user leaves a field), announce them with a live region or role="alert"; for errors found on submit, move focus to an error summary or the first invalid field. Should note that role="alert" on text already present at page load may not be announced. Should provide a code example.
expectations: Associates the error message text with its input through aria-describedby (or aria-errormessage with a caveat) and sets aria-invalid="true" on the invalid field.
Explains that the error must be identified in text and not only by red color, citing 1.4.1 Use of Color and/or 3.3.1 Error Identification.
If it covers errors that appear dynamically without a focus change (for example when the user leaves a field), announces them with role="alert" or an aria-live region.
If it covers errors found on submit, moves focus to an error summary or the first invalid field. The answer covers the case it assumes, or both.
Does not recommend putting role="alert" on error text that is already in the page at load as the way to announce it.
Provides a code example that includes the input, the linked error element and aria-invalid.
sources: references/forms.md (when to use role="alert"; error summary with focus)

evals.prompt: How do I make an SVG icon accessible? It's just a decorative checkmark.
evals.expected_output: Should say that a purely decorative SVG should be hidden from assistive technology with aria-hidden="true" (and have no title or other name), and that a decorative icon needs no alternative text. focusable="false" is a separate attribute about keyboard focus (relevant to old browsers that made SVG focusable); it does not hide the icon from assistive technology and is not a substitute for aria-hidden="true". If the icon is inside a button or link, the control needs its own accessible name from other content. Should contrast with an informative icon, which needs a text alternative (for example role="img" with aria-label or a title, or visually hidden text).
expectations: Recommends aria-hidden="true" on the decorative SVG so it is not exposed to assistive technology.
Does not present focusable="false" as an alternative to aria-hidden="true" for hiding the icon from screen readers; if it mentions focusable="false", it describes it as controlling keyboard focus.
Says a decorative icon should not be given a text alternative (no title or aria-label), and contrasts that with an informative icon that does need a name.
If the icon sits inside a button or link, notes that the control still needs an accessible name from text or another source.

evals.prompt:
I'm using a `div` as a button: `
Submit
`. Is this accessible?
evals.expected_output: Should answer that it is not accessible as written: a div has no button role (4.1.2 Name, Role, Value), is not in the Tab order (no tabindex), and has no keyboard activation (2.1.1 Keyboard: needs Enter and Space handling). Should recommend replacing it with a native <button> (type="button" or "submit" as needed), which gives role, focus, name from content and Enter/Space activation for free, and say that if a div cannot be avoided it needs role="button", tabindex="0" and key handlers for Enter and Space plus focus styles.
expectations: Says the div is not accessible as written and names at least the missing role and the missing keyboard access (not focusable, no Enter/Space activation).
Recommends replacing it with a native <button> as the preferred fix and explains that the native element supplies role, focus and keyboard activation.
If it offers a div fallback, includes role="button", tabindex="0" and handling for both Enter and Space.
Does not say that adding only tabindex="0" or only role="button" is enough.
sources: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/read-me-first/ (first rule of ARIA: use a native element when one exists)

evals.prompt: What is the difference between WCAG A, AA, and AAA?
evals.expected_output: Should explain that the levels are cumulative: A is the minimum level of conformance; AA includes all A and AA criteria; AAA includes all A, AA and AAA criteria. Should say that AA is the level most laws, policies and contracts name as the target, without calling it a universal global standard, and that W3C does not recommend requiring AAA as a general policy for entire sites because not all AAA criteria can be satisfied for some content (individual AAA criteria can still be adopted where they fit).
expectations: Explains that levels are cumulative: AA means meeting all A and AA success criteria, and AAA means meeting A, AA and AAA.
Describes Level A as the minimum level of conformance.
Says AA is the level that laws, policies and contracts commonly target, as a statement about common practice rather than a W3C rule.
Says AAA is not recommended as a general requirement for whole sites because some content cannot satisfy every AAA criterion, while individual AAA criteria can be applied where they fit.
Does not claim that AA is mandatory everywhere or is a single global legal standard, and does not claim AAA is required by WCAG.
sources: data/legal-framework.csv (laws name different versions and levels)

evals.prompt: How should I structure headings on a webpage?
evals.expected_output: Should recommend descriptive headings that state the topic or purpose of each section (WCAG 2.4.6, level AA), and a heading hierarchy (h1-h6) that reflects the structure of the content and is marked up with real heading elements rather than visual styling (1.3.1, level A). May recommend avoiding skipped heading levels as helpful guidance for navigation (W3C WAI says skipping ranks can be confusing and should be avoided where possible, and that it is fine to skip ranks when closing subsections), and may suggest a single main h1 as a common convention. Must not present 'exactly one H1' or 'never skip a heading level' as WCAG requirements.
expectations: Recommends headings that describe the topic or purpose of their section, citing 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (AA) or equivalent wording.
Says the heading levels should reflect the structure of the content and be real heading elements (h1-h6) instead of styled text, citing 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A) or equivalent wording.
If it advises not skipping levels or using one h1, frames it as guidance or convention for navigation, not as a WCAG requirement.
Does not state that WCAG requires exactly one h1, or that WCAG forbids skipping a heading level.

evals.prompt: What is an accessible name and how is it calculated?
evals.expected_output: Should explain that the accessible name is the text a control or element is announced by, computed by the browser using the Accessible Name and Description Computation (accname). In broad order: aria-labelledby first (referenced elements' text), then aria-label, then the native label of the host language (for example a <label> for an input, alt for an image, <caption> for a table), then name from content for roles that allow it (button, link, heading, tab...), and finally title as a last-resort tooltip fallback. Empty sources are skipped, and hidden content is normally left out, except when it is reached through aria-labelledby (or aria-describedby), where hidden referenced content does count. Should say it is not the same as the visible text (2.5.3 Label in Name asks that the name contain the visible label) and that it can be checked in the browser accessibility tree. Should not claim that visible text always wins over aria-label, or that aria-label is a substitute for a visible label.
expectations: Defines the accessible name as the name assistive technology exposes for an element, computed by the browser from several sources.
Gives an order of precedence in which aria-labelledby comes before aria-label, which comes before native sources such as a <label> or alt, and then name from content, with title only as a fallback.
Notes that name from content applies only to roles that allow it (for example button, link, heading).
Says empty sources are skipped and hidden content is normally left out of the name, except when the hidden element is referenced through aria-labelledby, where it still contributes.
Mentions that the name should contain the visible label text (2.5.3 Label in Name) or that it can be inspected in the browser accessibility tree.
Does not claim that aria-label always overrides aria-labelledby, or that visible text content always wins over aria-label.

evals.prompt: Is there a way to test accessibility automatically in CI/CD?
evals.expected_output: Should list tools that run in CI such as axe-core (via @axe-core/cli, @axe-core/playwright, jest-axe), pa11y or pa11y-ci, and Lighthouse CI, and show or describe how to fail the build on violations. Should say that automated tests detect only a part of the possible WCAG issues, so manual keyboard and screen reader checks are still needed.
expectations: Names at least two real tools usable in CI, such as axe-core based tools, pa11y or Lighthouse, and says how to run them in a pipeline (a script, a Playwright or Jest test, or a workflow step).
Explains how to make the pipeline fail on violations or how to set a threshold.
States that automated checks cover only part of WCAG and that manual testing (keyboard, screen reader) is still needed.
Does not claim that a passing automated scan means the site conforms to WCAG.

evals.prompt: How do I make a skip link?
evals.expected_output:
Should provide code for a skip link as the first focusable element on the page, with an href to the id of the main content (for example Skip to main content and
), hidden visually until it receives keyboard focus (positioned off-screen or clipped, not display:none or visibility:hidden, which would remove it from the Tab order), made visible with :focus. Should mention that the target may need tabindex="-1" so focus moves there in all browsers, and that this implements SC 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A).
expectations: Provides a link that is the first focusable element and points to the id of the main content.
Hides it visually by off-screen or clipping techniques and shows it on :focus (or :focus-visible), and does not hide it with display:none or visibility:hidden.
Says the link target must exist; if it discusses moving focus to the target, mentions tabindex="-1" on the target when needed.
Cites 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A) or says that it is a way to bypass repeated blocks.

evals.prompt: What are some cognitive accessibility best practices?
evals.expected_output: Should give several practical practices such as plain, concrete language; clear, specific error messages that say how to fix the problem (3.3.1, 3.3.3); consistent navigation and identification (3.2.3, 3.2.4); letting users turn off, adjust or extend time limits (2.2.1); not forcing users to re-enter information (3.3.7, WCAG 2.2); easy authentication that does not rely on remembering or transcribing (3.3.8). Should distinguish WCAG requirements from broader guidance (for example the W3C Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities), noting that reading level (3.1.5) is AAA.
expectations: Gives at least four concrete practices, such as plain language, clear error messages with suggestions, consistent navigation, adjustable or extendable time limits, avoiding redundant entry, and accessible authentication.
Where it cites a success criterion, the ID and meaning match (for example 3.3.1 or 3.3.3 for errors, 3.2.3 for consistent navigation, 2.2.1 for time limits, 3.3.7 for redundant entry).
Separates what WCAG requires from broader best practice, for example by saying plain language or reading level is guidance or AAA (3.1.5) rather than an A or AA requirement.
Does not say that WCAG requires avoiding all time limits; it says users must be able to turn off, adjust or extend them (unless an exception applies).

evals.prompt: Do I need alt text on every image?
evals.expected_output: Should explain that every image needs a considered text alternative decision, not necessarily descriptive text: purely decorative images get an empty alt (alt="") so assistive technology skips them; informative images get a short alt that conveys the same information; functional images (a linked or button image) get alt that describes the action or destination; images of text carry that text; complex images (charts, diagrams) get a short alt plus a longer description nearby or linked. An img element should not omit the alt attribute altogether. Should refer to the W3C WAI alt decision tree and 1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A).
expectations: Says decorative images should have an empty alt (alt="") and not a description.
Says informative images need alt text that conveys the same information or purpose, and functional images (inside links or buttons) need alt that describes the action or destination.
Mentions a longer description for complex images such as charts or diagrams.
Says an img should not omit the alt attribute entirely, or explains that empty alt is different from a missing alt.
Does not answer simply "yes, describe every image" or "no, only some images need alt" without the decorative versus informative distinction.

evals.prompt: What's the difference between aria-hidden and display: none?
evals.expected_output: Should explain that display: none removes the element from rendering: it is not visible, is not in the accessibility tree and its content cannot receive focus. aria-hidden="true" only removes the element and its descendants from the accessibility tree exposed to assistive technology; the element stays visible on screen and, if it contains focusable elements, they remain focusable by keyboard. Therefore aria-hidden="true" must not be put on or around focusable elements (use inert, or hide with display:none/hidden, when both visual and AT hiding are intended). aria-hidden affects assistive technology in general, not only screen readers. Should note that visually-hidden (off-screen) text does the opposite: seen only by assistive technology.
expectations: Explains that display: none hides the element visually and from the accessibility tree, and also removes it from keyboard focus.
Explains that aria-hidden="true" only removes the element from the accessibility tree: it remains visible on screen and does not change whether it is focusable.
Warns against putting aria-hidden="true" on or around focusable elements, because a keyboard user can still focus something assistive technology cannot see.
Does not say that aria-hidden hides content from screen readers only without saying the content stays focusable and visible.
Does not say aria-hidden="true" prevents an element from receiving focus.

evals.prompt: How do I write a VPAT?
evals.expected_output: Should explain that a VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template, from ITI) is the template, and the filled-in document is the Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR). Should say how to fill it: choose the edition (WCAG, Revised Section 508, EN 301 549, or INT), evaluate the product against each criterion with real testing, and record for each criterion a conformance level (Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable, and for WCAG Level AAA Not Evaluated) with remarks that explain the result. Should say the report is a statement by the vendor based on its evaluation, with the evaluation method, product version and date, and is not a certification. Should say that the template in this repository is unofficial.
expectations: Explains that VPAT is the template and the completed document is the Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR).
Describes the process: pick the VPAT edition (WCAG, Section 508, EN 301 549 or international), test the product against each criterion and record a conformance level with remarks for each.
Lists the conformance terms used in the report (Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable, and Not Evaluated where allowed).
Says the ACR documents the vendor's own evaluation (methods, product version, date) and is not a certification or a legal guarantee.
Does not present the unofficial template of this skill as the official ITI VPAT, and does not say a VPAT guarantees conformance.
sources: templates/vpat-2.5-template.md (unofficial template based on the VPAT 2.5 structure; source for the «Not Evaluated» term, which the ITI page does not show)

evals.prompt: Are carousels accessible?
evals.expected_output: Should say a carousel can be accessible but needs care. If slides rotate automatically (start without user action, last more than five seconds, shown alongside other content) 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) requires a mechanism to pause, stop or hide it; the APG carousel pattern adds that rotation stops on keyboard focus and mouse hover and is not restarted automatically, and that the rotation control should be first in the Tab order. Controls must be keyboard operable (2.1.1) and have accessible names. Live region: aria-live="off" on the slide container while rotating automatically and "polite" when not rotating (APG), with aria-atomic="false". A carousel that never moves on its own has no 2.2.2 duty but still needs the other points. Should not say live regions are always required.
expectations: Says carousels can be made accessible but have several risks, and does not answer with a flat yes or no.
For auto-rotating carousels, says there must be a way to pause, stop or hide the movement (2.2.2), and notes that a carousel that does not move on its own does not trigger that criterion.
Says the previous, next and pause controls must be real, keyboard-operable controls with accessible names.
Says rotation should stop when keyboard focus enters the carousel and not restart unless the user asks (APG), and that it should also stop while the mouse is over it.
If it covers live regions, says they should be off while the carousel rotates automatically and polite when the user moves between slides, and does not say live regions must always be present.
